assertions.text: Fulfillment method splitting is represented as its own table — items with different fulfillment types (store pickup vs home delivery) cannot share a shipment.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 — Fulfillment Method Split exists with scenarios clearly showing separation: 'One home delivery, one pickup' results in '2' shipments with groups '[Shirt] → home delivery; [Mug] → store pickup'

assertions.text: Delivery address splitting is represented as its own table — items going to different addresses must be in separate shipments.
assertions.evidence: Table 4 — Multiple Delivery Addresses exists with scenario 'Two items, two addresses' showing 'Shirt → 123 Main St; Gift book → 456 Oak Ave' results in '2' shipments

assertions.text: Availability splitting is represented as its own table — in-stock items ship immediately, backordered/pre-ordered items ship when available.
assertions.evidence: Table 2 — Availability Split has columns 'Immediate shipment?' and 'Deferred shipment?' with scenarios like 'One in stock, one backordered' showing 'Shirt' immediate and 'Camera' deferred

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation (minimising shipments) is represented as its own table — choosing which warehouses to ship from to minimise total shipment count.
assertions.evidence: Table 3 — Inventory Distribution (Warehouse Selection) with scenario 'Fewer warehouses preferred over largest single stock' shows '6' items split into '2' shipments from Philadelphia and Washington, demonstrating minimisation rule

assertions.text: Companion product grouping is represented as its own table — paired items (e.g. camera body and lens) should ship together from the same location when possible.
assertions.evidence: Table 5 — Companion Products exists with opening statement 'Companion pairs should ship together from the same warehouse *if possible*' and scenario 'Only one warehouse stocks both' showing 'Shipped together?' = 'yes' from WH East

assertions.text: Fulfillment table covers at least: all items for home delivery, all items for store pickup, and a mix of delivery and pickup items.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 includes: 'All items home delivery' scenario, 'All items store pickup' scenario, and 'One home delivery, one pickup' scenario covering all three required cases

assertions.text: Delivery address table covers at least: all items to the same address, and items to different addresses.
assertions.evidence: Table 4 includes: 'All items, same address' with 'Shirt, Pants' both to '123 Main St', and 'Two items, two addresses' scenario covering both required cases

assertions.text: Availability table covers at least: all items in stock, a mix of in-stock and pre-order/backorder, and two backordered/pre-ordered items with different dates. Pre-order and backorder are recognised as equivalent for splitting semantics — either by comment, note, or by including both with the same rules.
assertions.evidence: Table 2 covers in-stock, mixed, and different dates scenarios. However, the equivalence requirement is not met: the table only includes 'Backordered items' column with no pre-order examples shown, no explicit comment noting equivalence, and no examples of both pre-order AND backorder items with the same rules as required by the assertion's three-option specification

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table covers at least: single warehouse has full quantity, multi-warehouse split needed, fewer-warehouse split preferred over more warehouses, and cannot fulfill (insufficient total stock).
assertions.evidence: Table 3 includes: 'One warehouse covers all' (Chicago: 4), 'Two warehouses needed', 'Fewer warehouses preferred over largest single stock' scenario, and 'Total available stock is insufficient' scenario with open question

assertions.text: Companion table covers at least: single warehouse has both companions, unavoidable split (no warehouse has both but both are available), and fulfillment not possible (one companion not available anywhere).
assertions.evidence: Table 5 covers 'Only one warehouse stocks both' and 'No warehouse stocks both (unavoidable split)' scenarios. However, it lacks the required 'fulfillment not possible' scenario where one companion item is completely unavailable (e.g., Camera body in WH East but Camera lens in no warehouse at all)

assertions.text: Scenario names describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: All scenario names describe business situations: 'All items home delivery', 'One home delivery, one pickup', 'Multiple backordered, different available dates', 'Fewer warehouses preferred over largest single stock', 'No warehouse stocks both (unavoidable split)' — all descriptive of actual business logic

assertions.text: Trigger tables represent multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous — not value sets like {delivery, pickup} which lose which item has which property.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 uses separate columns 'Home delivery items' and 'Store pickup items' making mapping clear (e.g. 'Shirt' in home column, 'Mug' in pickup column). Table 4 uses arrow notation: 'Shirt → 123 Main St; Gift book → 456 Oak Ave' and Table 5 uses warehouse-specific columns 'WH East: A qty' / 'WH East: B qty' — all unambiguously map items to properties

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Qty ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: Table 3 uses scalar column 'Qty needed' with values like '4', '6' and warehouse columns with numbers '6', '2', '0' instead of item names. 'From?' column shows 'Chicago: 4' (scalar allocation) not item lists

assertions.text: Column names use business/domain language (e.g. 'Shipments?' not 'Result?', 'Warehouse stock' not 'inventory_map'). The tables read as a specification a product person could review.
assertions.evidence: Column names across all tables use domain language: 'Shipment count?', 'Shipment groups?', 'Immediate shipment?', 'Deferred shipment?', 'Qty needed', 'Delivery address', 'Shipped together?' — all business terminology readable by product stakeholders

assertions.text: Output/expected columns end with '?' (e.g. 'Shipments?', 'Groups?') to distinguish them from input columns.
assertions.evidence: All output columns end with '?': Table 1 has 'Shipment count?' and 'Shipment groups?', Table 2 has 'Immediate shipment?' and 'Deferred shipment?', Table 3 has 'Shipments?' and 'From?', Table 4 has 'Shipments?' and 'Shipment groups?', Table 5 has 'Shipped together?' and 'From?'

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: Table 3 assignments all physically valid: 'One warehouse covers all' assigns 4 to Chicago which has 6; 'Two warehouses needed' assigns 2 to Chicago (has 2) and 2 to LA (has 3); 'No warehouse stocks both' in Table 5 assigns Camera body to WH East (has 5) and lens to WH West (has 4). All assignments respect stock availability

assertions.text: Multiple open questions are surfaced across the tables — ambiguities, edge cases, or product decisions that the requirements don't fully specify.
assertions.evidence: Response includes dedicated 'Open Questions' section with 5 distinct questions plus inline annotations: Table 2 last row marked '← open: one deferred shipment per ETA, or hold all until June?', Table 3 last row marked '← open: reject order, or partially fulfil...', and section covers 'Backorder ETAs', 'Companion + availability', 'Companion + address', 'Companion + warehouse selection', and 'Unfulfillable quantity'
